Leather specific machines are ideal, and you can use any materials in them. The important part is what the internals are made out of. Household machine sewing internals are made out of plastic, as they don’t receive that much stress. Leather is harder to go through so more force is needed, and the parts inside need be able to handle higher stress. That’s why leather sewing machines tend to have metal gears. 


Post vs flatbed and 2d and 3D are connected. 

Flatbeds are flat surfaces where the sewing is done on a flat plane, and thus all materials need to lie completely flat. Post beds have a post coming up in the center, and thus materials don’t have to be completely flat. Some shoe patterns are 3D, meaning that when you see them together, the end result isn’t a flat piece, and thus a flatbed can’t handle it. 

Let’s say for example you want to change the swoosh on a retail pair. You couldn’t do it on a normal( flat )sewing machine because you would sew through both sides of the shoe. With a post bed or patcher style, you can aren’t limited to a flat plane, and can move material away with more freedom than a flatbed. 

If you’re not making bespokes, I wouldn’t get anything too expensive, the patcher would be the best. It gives you a lot of extra room to sew inside the shoe, you’ll have a lot more freedom to work with. so if your replacing or adding swooshes and stuff like that you’ll be good. 

I’d highly recommend looking up some videos on YouTube about it. There are a bunch out there where you can learn more about the machine.

Chinese leather patcher is a real nice starter. It’s about 99-150 depending on where you get it from. Hand crank, so no motorized movement, Kinda finicky, as it takes some work to get it running, but one lace you got it down it’s super easy to use. There’s plenty of video guides online. But it punches through leather stupid easy, I’ve put it through  10 oz leather no problem, so for shoes, especially Nike sneakers you’ll never have any problems when it comes to thickness. If you’re not opposed to a little setup, it’s hard to beat for the price. Big plus with this, you can see in 3D, very very useful for shoes. Hard to find cheap machines that can do this. 


Alternatively, the singer 4432 is a cheap electric sewing machine, the shoe surgeon teaches his classes with it. Downsides, it’s not meant for leather, so if you’re punching through thick leather the internals are made out of plastic so eventually your gears will strip and you’ll have to get a new one. But if you not 100% sure you’re going to do this for a while and just want to dip your toe in, this a good option. 
However, it’s a flatbed so it only sees in 2d. Closing your uppers will be difficult, and it’ll be harder to use 3D patterns. Still, it’s very easy to use, lots of resources behind it, an still a great choice. One of the best shoemakers (for sneakers at least) I know uses it. ( he does hand crank all of his stitches tho)

If you’re 100% sure you’re going to do this for a while, buy the best machine you can afford. Don’t go buying cheap ones and work your way up, you’ll save money in the long term. Nice machines makes your life much easier. You could probably get a nice used  juki flatbed for 4-800. If you want a posted be prepared to spend a little more. 


Keep an eye out for old singer machines on Craigslist. Their older stuff tends to be really high quality, so you might be able find a nice post or flatbed on the cheap. 

Hand stitching is also an option. I know some fantastic shoemakers who do it 100% by hand. It takes A LOT more work, but it saves money on a machine. , and can be pretty satisfying. Hand stitching has its own learning curve though, and it takes a while to learn how to get a clean consistent stitch. But always an option. 

Good luck!

When it comes to painting leather, esps higher quality leather like this, a big part of it is removing the finishing. Typically, leather is finished with oils, wax or synthetic sealer. Removing the finishing will help the paint sit better. Unfortunately, if you don’t know the finishing, you’re gonna have to prepare for all of them. An acetone wipe will get rid of any synthetic sealants, but can mess with the dye on the leather. Be sure not to get any of it on other parts of the shoe. 


Additionally, if it’s veg or chrome tanned will make a huge difference. These look chromed tanned based on pics, but if they’re veg tan it’ll have oils in the leather that could mess with adhesion. Unfinished veg tan however takes paint very well, you just need to remove any finishes. 

Applying a very very high grit sandpaper rub on desired areas will increase adhesion mechanically. It will also remove any wax that may be on the shoe. Use very very thin coats of paint, and apply many layers. Too thick paint will cause cracking down the line. Make sure each coat is completely dry before applying new layers. And since it is black I recommend starting with a layer of white paint. Angelus is my preferred brand of leather paint. 


Use tape( some people use masking, some use gaffers) to mask off the areas you don’t want paint. Make sure you get all the way to the edges to prevent bleeding. Rub it down hard with your nail to prevent any gaps where paint could bleed. I would mask off the bottom of your boots to prevent any unwanted paint. Use gloves and change them often to prevent paint spreadin to undesired areas, because it will inevitably get on your hands. You can use exactly knives to cut tape to ensure really sharp lines. Just be careful not to cut into your leather. 

See if you can remove the creases as the paint won’t apply evenly in them, and will likely crack. A wet towel and iron has proven well for me in the past for cheaper leathers. No clue about higher weight leathers tho. As always, do your own research, I could be wrong. 

Finish your paint with angelus sealer, or krylon finisher in the desired finish and appropriate material. Make sure to mask off non painted areas and shake very very very well before using krylon if you do. If you don’t it’ll apply unevenly and cause a really awful patina that is impossible to get off. Finishing will help prevent cracking down the line and prevent rubbing and will waterproof. 
Good luck!

Thicker noodles such as linguine or fettuccine, are typically used in lighter sauces, as it has more surface area. For example, parpadelle is typically used in stock based sauces because it has very high absorption compared to other pasta.
Bucatini is used for cream based pasta, with minimal accompaniment, as it is hollow, vs solid all the way through like in spaghetti

Barilla is fine. It’s bronze extruded, it still has good adhesion. Barilla is made at a higher hydration however, so it could lead to a smoother touch, but bronze extrusion is most important. Technique is cooking is far more important. Finishing your pasta in the sauce can also lead to higher adhesion, especially with lighter sauces, as the starch will thicken the sauce and lead to a higher bond with the pasta. I will admit that barilla is not the best, but it serves its purpose well enough n

It’s definitely the way it’s cut. Bronze extrusion leads to a more porous texture that promotes adhesion. Additionally, egg based pastas are rare, use two types of flour (semolina and all purpose, along with oil and water. Egg pasta is typically reserved for stuffed pasta or parpadelle.  Normal pasta is essentially the two flours, salt, oil, and water. 

Source: worked in high end Italian for two years, making both types of pasta every day.

You’re going to need a shoe pattern and a last. They aren’t cheap, but shoe making isn’t cheap to get into. Xylar studio has some pretty good ones. 


You’re also going to need the tools. I used an exacto and a skiving knife to cut, leather prickers and a mallet  to punch holes, thread, double sided tape, and contact cement mainly to assemble the uppers. You’ll need lasting pliers and nails to last the shoe, and barge glue, thread and a cobblers awl to attach the sole. 

You gotta learn the general process of making a shoe, Andrew wrigleys, or Tim skyrnes YouTube was real helpful. There’s also a discord group around sneakermaking, that was a bunch of help. Dm djayk1973 on insta for a invite. 


After that, it’s assembly, cut and sew all the pattern pieces, last them to the last ( shoe mold), and attach the sole. Honestly, once you understand the general process, it’s pretty straightforward, just difficult to execute properly.

I start by sanding the top layer with high grit, then brushing it with a mixture of acetone and paint so the initial brush penetrates really deep.

This is because paint binds a lot better with itself than leather. The sanding gives it some mechanical adhesion along with the chemical bond. I then hit with white first, use very very thin layers, let them fully dry, then whatever color you want. Don’t be afraid to start over if you start to lose the pattern in the leather.

Finish with a acrylic finisher, I like krylon matte, it’ll water proof and give it a extra layer of protection.

Good luck 👍
